paras: The threats against Rev. Charles H. Thomas were anonymous letters sent in May and June 1903 to the pastor of the African Methodist Episcopal church at Belleville, Illinois, ordering him to leave town on penalty of personal injury. The first letter, by Thomas's account, reached him about two weeks before a Black schoolteacher named Wyatt was lynched at Belleville, and it prompted Thomas to warn Governor Yates. The threats drew notice after the governor's office denied receiving that warning and the letter was found in state files.

According to Thomas, the original warning was mailed to him on May 22, 1903. Headed "St. Louis, Mo." and signed "A CITIZEN," it accused "Charles Thomas, Colored" of having "drawn the color line" and of trying "to force the niggers on the white race." It gave him two weeks to leave Belleville or "meet your place in line with other good niggers," and Thomas noted that "the time for the trouble to begin is June 5."

According to the Republic, this letter and other warnings led Thomas to write to Governor Yates on June 2, enclosing a copy of the threat. Wyatt was lynched on the night of June 6; a wire brief said he was lynched "for shooting" the county school superintendent, Charles Hertel. Two days later a wire item reported that Thomas was "receiving letters warning him to leave town on penalty of personal injury."

Thomas then spoke at protest meetings in Chicago, where he said the mayor and sheriff of Belleville had refused his plea to protect Wyatt and blamed the governor's inaction for the lynching. At one meeting he told Black listeners to "sell their coats and buy guns" if the authorities did not stop the hanging and burning of Black men.

The governor's private secretary, Col. John D. Oglesby, denied that any letter from Thomas had reached the executive office and demanded a retraction. Soon afterward the June 2 letter turned up on a desk in the attorney general's office, bearing the executive file mark and the arrival date of June 3. No report identifying the writer of the warnings, of any attack on Thomas, or of his leaving Belleville was found.

In the white press the threats first appeared as a one-line item in news digests, printed in the Minneapolis Journal on June 8 and in the Grand Rapids Herald-Review of Minnesota on June 20, a few lines from a brief on the Wyatt lynching. The Grand Rapids paper called the pastor "Charles H. Thompson" and ran the same digest page again on June 27. The St. Louis Republic printed the letter in full on June 26 in a Springfield special that showed Thomas had warned the governor, and the Rock Island Argus carried the same finding under the headline "Thomas Was Right as to Belleville."

The St. Paul Appeal, a Black weekly, mentioned the threats in its June 27 report of a Quinn Chapel meeting in Chicago, describing "Rev. C. F. Thomas" as "several times warned to leave his home" because of his "outspoken condemnation" of the Wyatt murder. Where the white reports treated the threats as a news item or as evidence in a dispute with the governor's office, the Appeal set them within its denunciation of the Belleville "outlaws."

Accounts differ on what prompted the threats. The St. Paul Appeal tied them to Thomas's condemnation of the lynching, while the letter he copied to the governor was mailed before the lynching and charged him with drawing "the color line." Because the Republic printed the letter with Thomas's dated note, it is the more direct evidence for the first warning, though it does not rule out later warnings of the kind the Appeal described.
